questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.2(e), 2(h) · Agreement and contract
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly states the relationship between an agreement and a contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872?

readLink.label: Read: Agreement, contract and the s.2 ladder →

options.text: Every agreement is a contract, because s.2(e) defines an agreement as a set of promises forming the consideration for each other
options.explanation: This reads enforceability into s.2(e). Enforceability is added only by s.2(h); an agreement that fails s.10 stays an agreement and never becomes a contract.

options.text: Every contract is an agreement and every agreement is a contract, the two words being interchangeable in the Act
options.explanation: This treats the two circles as identical and leaves s.2(g) — the void agreement — with nothing to describe.

options.text: Every contract is an agreement, but every agreement is not a contract
options.explanation: Correct. Contract = agreement + enforceability at law (s.2(h)); an agreement not enforceable by law is void (s.2(g)) and so is an agreement that never becomes a contract.

options.text: An agreement becomes a contract only when it is reduced to writing and registered
options.explanation: This promotes the proviso to s.10 into the general rule. Writing, attestation or registration are required only where some other law requires them.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.2(g), 2(j) · Void agreement and void contract
questions.stem: A contract validly formed in January 2026 becomes impossible to perform in June 2026 because the promised act is prohibited by a change of law. In the language of section 2, the contract:

readLink.label: Read: Classifying contracts →

options.text: becomes void when it ceases to be enforceable — s.2(j)
options.explanation: Correct. It was a contract and then ceased to be enforceable, which is exactly the s.2(j) description; the trigger here is the second paragraph of s.56.

options.text: was void ab initio under s.2(g), the act having turned out to be unlawful
options.explanation: This backdates the defect. s.2(g) describes an agreement that was never enforceable at all — a minor's agreement, a wager — not one that failed later.

options.text: becomes voidable at the option of the promisor under s.2(i)
options.explanation: Voidability is the consequence of defective consent, not of supervening impossibility. Nobody here has an option; the contract simply ends.

options.text: remains a contract, only the promisor's liability in damages being extinguished
options.explanation: Frustration under s.56 kills the contract itself, and s.65 then requires restoration of advantages received; it does not leave a live contract with no remedy.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · s.2(a) · Offer versus invitation to offer
questions.stem: Which of the following is an OFFER (proposal) and not merely an invitation to offer?

readLink.label: Read: Offer, its kinds, and invitation to offer →

options.text: Goods displayed in a shop window with a price tag attached
options.explanation: The display is an invitation; the customer makes the offer at the counter and the shopkeeper may still refuse it.

options.text: An advertisement inviting tenders for the supply of stationery
options.explanation: A tender notice invites offers. The tenderer makes the offer; the inviter accepts one of them.

options.text: A prospectus issued by a company inviting the public to subscribe for its shares
options.explanation: A prospectus is an invitation to offer. The applicant offers by applying; the company accepts by allotment.

options.text: A newspaper announcement promising ₹10,000 to anyone who returns a lost briefcase
options.explanation: Correct. This is a general offer capable of acceptance by performance under s.8 — the Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball principle.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · s.2(a) · Auction sales
questions.stem: At an auction the auctioneer displays a lot and invites bids. Vikram bids ₹2,00,000 and, before the fall of the hammer, withdraws his bid. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Offer, its kinds, and invitation to offer →

options.text: Vikram cannot withdraw, because his bid was an acceptance of the auctioneer's offer
options.explanation: This treats the auctioneer's call for bids as an offer. It is an invitation to offer, so the bid cannot be an acceptance.

options.text: Vikram may withdraw, because the auctioneer's call for bids is an invitation to offer and the bid is only an offer until the hammer falls
options.explanation: Correct. Acceptance occurs at the fall of the hammer; until then the bidder's offer is revocable like any other offer under s.5.

options.text: Vikram may withdraw only if the auction was expressly advertised as being without reserve
options.explanation: A reserve price affects whether the auctioneer must sell; it has nothing to do with when a bid becomes irrevocable.

options.text: The withdrawal operates as a counter offer which the auctioneer may accept or reject
options.explanation: A withdrawal proposes no new terms at all, so it cannot be a counter offer.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.2(b), 4 · Cross offers
questions.stem: On the same day, and each in ignorance of the other, P posts a letter to Q offering to sell his car for ₹3,50,000 and Q posts a letter to P offering to buy the same car for ₹3,50,000. The legal position is:

readLink.label: Read: Offer, its kinds, and invitation to offer →

options.text: There is no contract, because cross offers are not an acceptance of each other
options.explanation: Correct. Each letter is an independent proposal; neither signifies assent to the other, so the s.2(b) step from proposal to promise is never taken.

options.text: There is a contract, the terms of the two letters being identical
options.explanation: This treats identity of terms as consent. Consent requires an act of assent to the other's proposal, not a coincidence of wishes.

options.text: There is a contract, formed when the later of the two letters is delivered
options.explanation: Delivery of a second proposal completes the communication of that proposal (s.4); it does not turn it into an acceptance.

options.text: There is a voidable contract at the option of whichever party posted first
options.explanation: Voidability arises only from defective consent under ss.19 and 19A; there is no contract here at all to be avoided.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.2(b), 7 · Silence is not acceptance
questions.stem: U writes to V: 'I offer you my scooter for ₹35,000. If I hear nothing from you by Sunday, I shall take it that you have accepted.' V says nothing and does nothing. On Monday the position is:

readLink.label: Read: Acceptance — ss.7 and 8 →

options.text: There is a contract, V's silence being assent because the offeror prescribed the manner of acceptance
options.explanation: s.7 lets the offeror prescribe a manner; it does not let him prescribe that doing nothing counts as assent.

options.text: There is a contract, but it is voidable at V's option
options.explanation: Voidability presupposes a contract formed with defective consent. Here no acceptance was ever communicated, so nothing was formed.

options.text: There is no contract, because the offer was not made in writing signed by both parties
options.explanation: Writing and signature are not requirements of a valid offer; the flaw here is the absence of any acceptance.

options.text: There is no contract, because an offeror cannot impose a duty to reply and silence is not acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. Acceptance must be signified (s.2(b)) and communicated; Felthouse v Bindley is the authority.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · s.6(4) · Death of the proposer
questions.stem: A makes a proposal to B on 1 June. A dies on 4 June. Unaware of the death, B posts his acceptance on 6 June. The position is:

readLink.label: Read: Communication, revocation and lapse — ss.3 to 6 →

options.text: There is no contract, the death of the proposer terminating the proposal automatically
options.explanation: This drops the words that matter. s.6(4) revokes the proposal by death or insanity only if the fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance.

options.text: There is a contract, because under s.6(4) death ends a proposal only if the fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. B accepted in genuine ignorance, so the proposal was still alive and A's estate is bound.

options.text: There is a contract only if A's legal representatives afterwards ratify it
options.explanation: No ratification is needed; s.37 makes the promisor's representatives bound unless the contract requires personal performance.

options.text: The contract is voidable at the option of A's legal representatives
options.explanation: Death gives the representatives no option to avoid. Their only escape is a contract of personal skill under s.40.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · s.7 · Acceptance not in the prescribed manner
questions.stem: R's proposal states that it must be accepted 'by registered post only'. S accepts by e-mail. R reads the e-mail and says nothing for three weeks. The position is:

readLink.label: Read: Acceptance — ss.7 and 8 →

options.text: There is no contract, a prescribed manner of acceptance being mandatory and a deviant acceptance a nullity
options.explanation: That is the English rule, not s.7. Under s.7 a deviant acceptance is good unless the proposer objects.

options.text: There is no contract, but R may make a fresh proposal on the same terms if he wishes
options.explanation: This assumes the acceptance was a nullity. It was effective the moment R let the reasonable time pass without objecting.

options.text: There is a contract, because R failed within a reasonable time to insist on the prescribed manner and so accepted the acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. The closing words of s.7(2) put the burden on the proposer to object within a reasonable time; silence validates the acceptance.

options.text: There is a contract, because a prescribed manner of acceptance is merely a recommendation and never binds the acceptor
options.explanation: It does bind, in the limited sense that the proposer may insist on it — the acceptor cannot ignore it and be safe.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · s.6(2) · Lapse of an offer by efflux of time
questions.stem: Chandrika's offer letter is dated 11 May 2026 and states: 'This offer is open for acceptance for twenty-one days from the date of this letter.' Counting the period from (and excluding) the date of the letter, the last date on which a valid acceptance can be posted is:

readLink.label: Read: Communication, revocation and lapse — ss.3 to 6 →

options.explanation: This counts 11 May itself as day 1, which shortens the period the offeror actually gave by a day.

options.text: 11 June 2026
options.explanation: This reads 'twenty-one days' as one calendar month. The offer names days, and days are counted as days.

options.text: 2 June 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one: it counts twenty-two days from 11 May.

options.text: 1 June 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Day 1 is 12 May, so the twenty-first day is 1 June 2026; after that the proposal is revoked by lapse of time under s.6(2).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.4, 5 · Postal rule — when the contract is made
questions.stem: Devika, at Pune, posts a proposal on 2 February 2026 to sell a lathe to Firoz at Surat; Firoz receives it on 6 February. Firoz posts his acceptance on 10 February and it reaches Devika on 14 February. Devika had posted a letter revoking the proposal on 8 February, which reached Firoz on 12 February. A contract came into existence on:

readLink.label: Read: Communication, revocation and lapse — ss.3 to 6 →

options.text: 6 February 2026, when the proposal was communicated to Firoz
options.explanation: Communication of the proposal only makes it capable of acceptance (s.4); it forms nothing by itself.

options.text: 10 February 2026, when Firoz posted his acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. Communication of an acceptance is complete as against the proposer when it is posted, and Devika's revocation reached Firoz only on 12 February — too late under s.5.

options.text: 12 February 2026, when Devika's revocation reached Firoz
options.explanation: This treats the revocation as effective. A revocation binds the offeree when it reaches him, and by 12 February the contract had already been concluded on 10 February.

options.text: 14 February 2026, when the acceptance reached Devika
options.explanation: That is the date the communication is complete as against the ACCEPTOR. Against the proposer it was complete on posting.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.4, 5 · Revocation of an acceptance
questions.stem: On the same facts, Firoz changes his mind on 11 February 2026. His revocation of the acceptance will be effective only if it reaches Devika not later than:

readLink.label: Read: Communication, revocation and lapse — ss.3 to 6 →

options.text: 10 February 2026
options.explanation: That is the date of posting — the deadline for the OFFEROR to revoke his proposal, not for the acceptor to revoke his acceptance.

options.text: 12 February 2026
options.explanation: This borrows the date on which the offeror's revocation happened to arrive; it has nothing to do with Firoz's deadline.

options.text: 14 February 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Communication of the acceptance is complete as against Firoz when it reaches Devika, so under s.5 he may revoke at any time before or at that moment — 14 February.

options.text: 13 February 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one. The Act allows revocation up to and including the moment the acceptance reaches the proposer.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · s.2(d) · At the desire of the promisor
questions.stem: X builds a market at the order of the District Collector. The shopkeepers who later occupy the shops promise X a commission on their sales. X sues on the promise. He will:

readLink.label: Read: Consideration — s.2(d) →

options.text: fail, because the construction was not done at the desire of the shopkeepers
options.explanation: Correct. s.2(d) requires the act to be done at the desire of the PROMISOR; an act done at a third party's order is no consideration for their promise.

options.text: succeed, because past consideration is good consideration in India
options.explanation: Past consideration is good only if the past act was itself done at the promisor's desire. That first condition fails here.

options.text: succeed, because s.2(d) allows consideration to move from any person
options.explanation: That limb addresses WHO furnishes the consideration, not AT WHOSE DESIRE it was furnished.

options.text: fail, because a promise to pay an unquantified commission is void for uncertainty under s.29
options.explanation: A commission expressed as a share of sales is capable of being made certain, so s.29 is not the obstacle.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · s.2(d) · Consideration from a stranger
questions.stem: What follows from the words 'the promisee or any other person' in section 2(d)?

readLink.label: Read: Consideration — s.2(d) →

options.text: Consideration is unnecessary whenever a third person is involved in the transaction
options.explanation: The words change who may supply the consideration; they never dispense with consideration.

options.text: Consideration may move from a person who is not a party to the promise, so a stranger to the CONSIDERATION may sue in India
options.explanation: Correct. This is the Indian departure from English law, illustrated by Chinnaya v Ramayya.

options.text: A stranger to the CONTRACT may sue upon it in India
options.explanation: This confuses the two doctrines. Privity of contract survives in India; only privity of consideration was abolished.

options.text: The promisor may recover the consideration from a third person if the promisee defaults
options.explanation: s.2(d) says nothing about recovery from third persons; it is a definition of consideration.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · Explanation 2 to s.25 · Adequacy of consideration
questions.stem: A agrees to sell a horse worth ₹1,00,000 for ₹1,000, his consent being freely given. The agreement is:

readLink.label: Read: Consideration — s.2(d) →

options.text: void for want of consideration
options.explanation: There is consideration — ₹1,000. The complaint is about its amount, which is a different question.

options.text: void, the consideration being illusory
options.explanation: Illusory means unreal or impossible, such as a promise to bring the dead to life. ₹1,000 is real money.

options.text: a valid contract, inadequacy of consideration not by itself invalidating an agreement, though it is evidence on the question of free consent
options.explanation: Correct. Explanation 2 to s.25 says exactly this, and the Act's own illustration uses these very figures in miniature.

options.text: voidable at A's option because the consideration is grossly inadequate
options.explanation: Inadequacy is evidence of absent free consent, not an independent ground of avoidance. Without coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation there is no option to avoid.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · s.25(1) · Natural love and affection
questions.stem: An elder brother, out of affection, orally promises his younger brother ₹5,00,000 and then refuses to pay. The younger brother's suit will:

readLink.label: Read: No consideration no contract — s.25 →

options.text: fail, because s.25(1) requires the agreement to be in writing and registered as well as made between near relations out of natural love and affection
options.explanation: Correct. All the elements of s.25(1) are cumulative; an oral promise, however affectionate, is outside the exception.

options.text: succeed under s.25(1), the parties standing in a near relation to each other
options.explanation: Near relation is only one of four requirements. Writing, registration and actual natural love and affection must also be present.

options.text: succeed, because natural love and affection is itself good consideration under s.2(d)
options.explanation: Affection is not consideration. s.25(1) is an exception to the requirement of consideration, not an example of it.

options.text: fail, because an agreement between brothers can never be enforced by a court
options.explanation: Relationship is no bar. A registered written promise between the same brothers would be perfectly enforceable.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · s.25(2) · Past voluntary service
questions.stem: Y finds Z's wallet in the street and returns it, expecting nothing. Z afterwards promises Y ₹2,000 for his trouble, then refuses to pay. Y's suit will:

readLink.label: Read: No consideration no contract — s.25 →

options.text: fail, past consideration being no consideration under Indian law
options.explanation: Past consideration IS good in India where the act was done at the promisor's desire; and even a voluntary past act is saved by s.25(2).

options.text: succeed under s.70, the return of the wallet being a non-gratuitous act
options.explanation: s.70 requires that the act was done without any intention of acting gratuitously. Y expected nothing, so s.70 is closed to him.

options.text: fail, because the promise was not in writing and registered
options.explanation: Writing and registration are demanded by s.25(1), not by s.25(2). A promise to compensate past voluntary service needs no formality.

options.text: succeed under s.25(2), the promise being to compensate a person who had already voluntarily done something for the promisor
options.explanation: Correct. This is the second exception in s.25, and it is what rescues Y despite the absence of consideration.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · Privity of contract
questions.stem: A contract between M and N provides that N shall pay ₹50,000 to O, who is not a party to it. O sues N. O's suit will ordinarily:

readLink.label: Read: Privity of contract and of consideration →

options.text: succeed, because s.2(d) permits consideration to move from any person
options.explanation: That abolishes privity of consideration, not privity of contract. O's problem is that he is not a party.

options.text: succeed, because the contract was expressly made for O's benefit
options.explanation: A benefit conferred by a contract does not by itself confer a right to sue on it — that is precisely what Dunlop v Selfridge decides.

options.text: fail for want of privity of contract, unless O can bring himself within an exception such as a trust or charge created in his favour
options.explanation: Correct. The rule bars him; the way in is one of the recognised exceptions — trust or charge, family arrangement, acknowledgement, assignment, covenant running with land, agency.

options.text: fail, because a promise to pay money to a third person is unlawful under s.23
options.explanation: There is nothing unlawful in agreeing to pay a third person. The obstacle is procedural standing, not legality.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.11 · Minor's agreement is void ab initio
questions.stem: A minor mortgages his house to secure a loan and, on attaining majority, refuses to repay. Following Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose:
questions.sourceRef: s. 11; Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose

readLink.label: Read: Capacity and the minor — s.11 →

options.text: the mortgage is voidable at the minor's option, and the lender may at least recover the principal
options.explanation: This treats a minor's agreement as voidable. It is void ab initio, and there is no option to be exercised.

options.text: the mortgage is void ab initio, and the lender can recover neither the money advanced nor enforce the security
options.explanation: Correct. That is the exact holding: a minor's agreement is void from the beginning, and ss.64 and 65 do not fasten liability on him.

options.text: the mortgage is valid, the minor having received full value for it
options.explanation: Receipt of value cannot supply capacity. s.11 is a bar on competence, not on fairness.

options.text: the mortgage is enforceable to the extent of the minor's benefit under s.68
options.explanation: s.68 is confined to NECESSARIES supplied, and gives a claim against the minor's property; a loan on mortgage is not a supply of necessaries.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.11 · Ratification after majority
questions.stem: Three months after attaining majority, a person writes to his creditor confirming a loan taken during his minority and promising to repay it. The confirmation:

readLink.label: Read: Capacity and the minor — s.11 →

options.text: is of no effect — a void agreement cannot be ratified, and a fresh promise needs fresh consideration
options.explanation: Correct. Consideration given during minority cannot support a promise made after majority; only a wholly new contract will bind him.

options.text: is a valid ratification and binds him from the date of the original loan
options.explanation: Ratification presupposes something capable of being ratified. A void agreement is a legal nothing.

options.text: binds him for the interest that accrued after majority, though not for the principal
options.explanation: There is no such split. The original transaction is void in its entirety, interest included.

options.text: binds him, because the Limitation Act permits a debt to be acknowledged in writing
options.explanation: An acknowledgement extends the limitation period for an existing enforceable debt; it cannot create liability where none ever existed.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.68 · Necessaries supplied to a minor
questions.stem: A trader supplies a minor with school textbooks and uniforms suited to his condition in life. The price is unpaid. The trader may:

readLink.label: Read: Capacity and the minor — s.11 →

options.text: sue the minor personally on the contract for the price
options.explanation: There is no contract to sue on; and s.68 expressly gives a claim against property, not a personal decree.

options.text: sue the minor's father, who is liable for his son's contracts
options.explanation: A parent is not liable for a minor's contracts unless the minor contracted as his agent, which is not stated here.

options.text: recover nothing, an agreement with a minor being void
options.explanation: The agreement is void, but s.68 creates a separate quasi-contractual claim precisely for necessaries.

options.text: recover the price from the minor's property under s.68, but obtain no personal decree against the minor
options.explanation: Correct. s.68 reimburses the supplier of necessaries out of the incapable person's property; a minor with no property pays nothing.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.11 · Position of a minor — the false statement
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement of a minor's position under the Act?

readLink.label: Read: Capacity and the minor — s.11 →

options.text: A minor may be admitted to the benefits of a partnership with the consent of all the partners
options.explanation: This is correct law (s.30 of the Partnership Act) — so it is not the answer.

options.text: A minor who misrepresents his age is estopped from afterwards pleading his minority
options.explanation: Correct choice — this statement is WRONG. There is no estoppel against a minor; he may still plead minority, though equity may order restoration of what is traceable in his hands.

options.text: A minor may act as an agent and bind his principal without incurring personal liability
options.explanation: This is correct law — a minor's want of capacity affects contracts made for himself, not acts done for a principal.

options.text: A minor may enforce a contract entered into for his benefit by his lawful guardian within the guardian's authority
options.explanation: This is correct law — the incapacity is a shield for the minor, not a bar on benefits secured for him.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · ss.26, 28, 29 · Agreements expressly declared void
questions.stem: Which of the following agreements is NOT void?

readLink.label: Read: Agreements expressly declared void — ss.26 to 30 →

options.text: An agreement in restraint of the marriage of an adult
options.explanation: Void under s.26; only a restraint on the marriage of a minor falls outside the section.

options.text: An agreement by which a party is absolutely restricted from enforcing his rights in the ordinary tribunals
options.explanation: Void under s.28(a) to that extent.

options.text: An agreement the meaning of which is not certain and is not capable of being made certain
options.explanation: Void under s.29 for uncertainty.

options.text: An agreement to refer future disputes between the parties to arbitration
options.explanation: Correct. This is expressly saved by the first Exception to s.28 and is a valid agreement.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.15 · What amounts to coercion
questions.stem: Which of the following amounts to coercion within the meaning of section 15?

readLink.label: Read: Coercion and undue influence — ss.15 and 16 →

options.text: Threatening to file a civil suit for the recovery of a debt actually due
options.explanation: A threat to do what one is lawfully entitled to do is not coercion; no act forbidden by penal law and no unlawful detention is involved.

options.text: Refusing to deal further with a party unless he agrees to a higher price for future supplies
options.explanation: Refusing to contract is lawful. Hard bargaining is neither coercion nor undue influence.

options.text: Unlawfully detaining the goods of a person, to his prejudice, in order to make him sign an agreement
options.explanation: Correct. This is the second limb of s.15 — unlawful detention of property with the intention of causing a person to enter into an agreement.

options.text: Persuading an elderly relative over whom one has influence to sell property at a low price
options.explanation: That is undue influence under s.16, not coercion. The distinguishing feature is a dominating relationship rather than a threat or detention.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.16(3) · Burden of proof in undue influence
questions.stem: A spiritual adviser induces his devotee to gift him almost the whole of her property. In a suit to set the gift aside:

readLink.label: Read: Coercion and undue influence — ss.15 and 16 →

options.text: the burden lies on the adviser to prove that the gift was not induced by undue influence, the transaction being unconscionable on its face
options.explanation: Correct. Once domination plus an unconscionable bargain appear, s.16(3) shifts the burden onto the dominant party.

options.text: the devotee must prove both that the adviser dominated her will and that he obtained an unfair advantage
options.explanation: She must show enough to raise the presumption; she does not carry the whole burden once the transaction is unconscionable.

options.text: the gift is void ab initio, so no question of burden of proof arises
options.explanation: Undue influence makes a transaction VOIDABLE at the option of the influenced party (s.19A), not void.

options.text: the gift stands, a completed gift being protected by Explanation 1 to s.25
options.explanation: Explanation 1 protects a gift from attack for WANT OF CONSIDERATION only. It gives no protection against undue influence.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.16(2) · Where undue influence is not presumed
questions.stem: In which of the following relationships is undue influence NOT presumed?

readLink.label: Read: Coercion and undue influence — ss.15 and 16 →

options.text: Trustee and beneficiary
options.explanation: A fiduciary relation squarely within s.16(2)(a); the presumption applies.

options.text: Advocate and client
options.explanation: A classic fiduciary relation; the presumption applies.

options.text: Guardian and ward
options.explanation: Real authority over the other within s.16(2)(a); the presumption applies.

options.text: Husband and wife in the ordinary case
options.explanation: Correct. No presumption arises between spouses as such; undue influence must be proved on the facts, as it must between landlord and tenant or arm's-length creditor and debtor.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · ss.18, 19 · Consequences of misrepresentation
questions.stem: A seller honestly, but without adequate information, asserts that a machine has a rated output of 500 units an hour. The buyer contracts in reliance and finds the output is 300. The buyer may:

readLink.label: Read: Fraud and misrepresentation — ss.17 to 19 →

options.text: rescind the contract, or insist that it be performed and that he be put in the position he would have been in had the representation been true, but he cannot claim damages
options.explanation: Correct. That is the s.19 remedy set for misrepresentation; damages are the additional consequence of fraud, not of an innocent misstatement.

options.text: rescind the contract and also claim damages, the statement being fraudulent
options.explanation: Fraud under s.17 requires that the maker did not believe the statement true, or intended to deceive. Here he believed it.

options.text: do nothing, because a statement about future output is an expression of opinion
options.explanation: A rated output asserted as a present fact about the machine is a statement of fact, not an opinion.

options.text: claim damages only, rescission being barred once the machine has been delivered
options.explanation: Delivery does not bar rescission; only affirmation, impossibility of restitution, third-party rights or undue delay do.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · Explanation to s.17 · Silence as fraud
questions.stem: In which of the following is SILENCE fraud within the meaning of section 17?

readLink.label: Read: Fraud and misrepresentation — ss.17 to 19 →

options.text: A shopkeeper does not tell a customer that the same article is available more cheaply in the next street
options.explanation: There is no duty to speak about a competitor's price; mere silence as to facts affecting willingness is not fraud.

options.text: A person applying for a life insurance policy does not disclose a serious illness for which he is under treatment
options.explanation: Correct. Insurance is a contract uberrimae fidei, so there is a duty to speak, and silence becomes fraud.

options.text: A seller of a horse does not disclose that it is unsound, no question having been asked and there being no relationship between the parties
options.explanation: This is the Explanation's own paradigm of mere silence, which is not fraud.

options.text: A landlord does not tell a prospective tenant that rents in the locality have recently fallen
options.explanation: A market movement equally discoverable by the tenant raises no duty to speak.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · Exception to s.19 · Means of discovering the truth
questions.stem: Consent is obtained by an innocent misrepresentation, and the misled party could have discovered the truth with ordinary diligence from documents freely offered to him. The contract is:

readLink.label: Read: Fraud and misrepresentation — ss.17 to 19 →

options.text: voidable at his option, the means of discovering the truth being irrelevant once a false statement is proved
options.explanation: That is the position for ACTIVE FRAUD, where the Exception does not apply. For misrepresentation, the means of discovery defeat the claim.

options.text: void, because there was no consensus ad idem between the parties
options.explanation: Misrepresentation does not destroy consensus; it makes consent unfree, which at most produces voidability.

options.text: not voidable, because the Exception to s.19 denies relief where the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence
options.explanation: Correct. The Exception covers consent caused by misrepresentation or by silence amounting to fraud — never active fraud.

options.text: voidable, but only if he sues within three years of the contract
options.explanation: Limitation governs when he may sue, not whether the Exception applies. The Exception removes the right itself.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.20 · Bilateral mistake of fact
questions.stem: Both parties contract for the sale of a specific consignment which, unknown to either of them, had already perished before the agreement was made. The agreement is:

readLink.label: Read: Mistake — ss.20 to 22 →

options.text: void under s.20, both parties being under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement
options.explanation: Correct. This is mistake as to the existence of the subject matter (res extincta) — the paradigm bilateral mistake.

options.text: valid, the seller bearing the risk of loss until delivery
options.explanation: Risk allocation presupposes a subject matter that existed when the bargain was struck. Here there was none.

options.text: voidable at the buyer's option under s.19
options.explanation: s.19 deals with coercion, fraud and misrepresentation. Nobody misled anybody here.

options.text: void under s.56, performance having become impossible
options.explanation: The right idea in the wrong section: the second paragraph of s.56 deals with impossibility arising AFTER the contract is made. The goods had already perished.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.21 · Mistake of law
questions.stem: Two parties enter into a contract under a mistaken view of a law in force in India. The contract is:

readLink.label: Read: Mistake — ss.20 to 22 →

options.text: void under s.20, a mistake of law being a mistake as to a matter essential to the agreement
options.explanation: s.20 is confined to mistakes of FACT; a mistake of Indian law is expressly dealt with by s.21.

options.text: voidable at the option of the party who was mistaken
options.explanation: s.21 says the contract is 'not voidable' for a mistake as to Indian law — the exact opposite.

options.text: valid, because s.21 provides that a contract is not voidable on account of a mistake as to any law in force in India
options.explanation: Correct. Only a mistake as to a law NOT in force in India is treated like a mistake of fact. Note that money paid under a mistake of law is still recoverable under s.72.

options.text: void, on the principle that ignorance of the law excuses no one
options.explanation: The maxim explains WHY s.21 says what it does, but the statutory consequence is validity, not voidness.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.23 · Object opposed to public policy
questions.stem: Which of the following agreements is void as being opposed to public policy?

readLink.label: Read: Lawful object and consideration — s.23 →

options.text: An agreement to compound an offence which the law expressly permits to be compounded
options.explanation: Compounding a compoundable offence is permitted by law; only stifling a NON-compoundable prosecution offends public policy.

options.text: An agreement to refer an existing question between the parties to arbitration
options.explanation: Expressly saved by the second Exception to s.28, and in no way opposed to public policy.

options.text: An agreement by a partner not to carry on any business other than that of the firm while he is a partner
options.explanation: Expressly permitted by s.11(2) of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 and therefore outside s.27 as well.

options.text: An agreement to pay money to a person for procuring a government appointment for the promisee's son
options.explanation: Correct. Trafficking in public offices is a settled head of public policy under s.23, and the agreement is void.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.27 · Restraint of trade and the goodwill exception
questions.stem: Sharda sells the goodwill of her bakery in Nashik to Tarun and agrees not to carry on a bakery anywhere in India for the next ten years. The covenant is:

readLink.label: Read: Agreements expressly declared void — ss.26 to 30 →

options.text: wholly valid, a restraint accompanying the sale of goodwill being outside s.27 altogether
options.explanation: The Exception is not unlimited. It saves a restraint only within SPECIFIED LOCAL LIMITS that the court regards as reasonable.

options.text: void under s.27, the restraint not being confined to specified local limits that the court would regard as reasonable
options.explanation: Correct. A nationwide restraint to protect the goodwill of a single Nashik bakery goes far beyond what the Exception permits.

options.text: valid, because a restraint of trade is enforceable in India whenever it is reasonable between the parties
options.explanation: That is the English test. s.27 voids restraints outright, and reasonableness matters only inside the statutory exceptions.

options.text: voidable at Sharda's option, a restraint of trade being an unfair advantage taken of a seller
options.explanation: s.27 makes such an agreement void 'to that extent'; it does not create an option to avoid.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · s.30 · Wagering agreements
questions.stem: Which of the following is a wagering agreement within section 30?

readLink.label: Read: Agreements expressly declared void — ss.26 to 30 →

options.text: A fire insurance policy taken by the owner of a warehouse on his own stock
options.explanation: The insured has an insurable interest in the goods, so there is an interest beyond the stake and the contract is contingent, not a wager.

options.text: A subscription of ₹2,00,000 towards a prize to be awarded to the winner of a horse race
options.explanation: Expressly carved out of s.30, the amount being ₹500 or upwards.

options.text: An agreement that one party shall pay the other ₹10,000 if it rains in Chennai on 15 August, and the other shall pay him ₹10,000 if it does not
options.explanation: Correct. Every essential is present: an uncertain future event, mutual chances of gain and loss, no interest beyond the stake, and no control over the event.

options.text: A contract to purchase shares which the parties intend to have actually delivered and paid for
options.explanation: A genuine purchase is not a wager, however much the price may move afterwards; only a settlement of differences without delivery would be.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.55 · Accepting delayed performance
questions.stem: Time is of the essence of a supply contract. The supplier delivers three weeks late and the buyer accepts the delivery without saying anything at the time. The buyer now claims compensation for the delay. He will:

readLink.label: Read: Performance — who, when and where →

options.text: succeed, because time was of the essence and the breach is admitted
options.explanation: The breach is admitted, but the third paragraph of s.55 attaches a condition to accepting late performance which the buyer did not satisfy.

options.text: fail, because a promisee who accepts performance at a time other than that agreed cannot claim compensation unless he gave notice of that intention at the time of acceptance
options.explanation: Correct. Acceptance without notice waives the claim to compensation for the delay.

options.text: succeed, because acceptance of late delivery does not amount to a waiver of any right
options.explanation: It does — s.55 says so expressly, unless notice is given at the time of acceptance.

options.text: fail, because where time is of the essence the only remedy is to avoid the contract, and the buyer chose not to
options.explanation: Avoidance is not the only remedy; compensation is available too, and would have been available here had notice been given.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.63 · Remission without consideration
questions.stem: A creditor to whom ₹5,00,000 is due agrees in writing to accept ₹3,00,000 in full satisfaction, and is paid that sum. He then sues for the balance. Under Indian law he will:

readLink.label: Read: Discharge of a contract →

options.text: fail, because s.63 allows a promisee to remit performance wholly or in part, and no consideration is needed for the remission
options.explanation: Correct. This is a settled departure from the English rule that part payment does not discharge the whole debt.

options.text: succeed, because a promise to accept less than the sum due is unsupported by consideration and is therefore void
options.explanation: That is the English position. s.63 expressly dispenses with consideration for a remission in India.

options.text: succeed, unless the remission was registered under s.25(1)
options.explanation: Registration is a requirement of s.25(1) for gratuitous promises made out of natural love and affection; it has nothing to do with s.63.

options.text: fail, but only if the debtor gave some fresh consideration for the reduction
options.explanation: No fresh consideration is required — that is the whole point of s.63.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.56 · What does not frustrate a contract
questions.stem: After a contract for the supply of imported components is made, import duty and freight rise so steeply that the supplier will make a heavy loss on performance. The supplier claims the contract is discharged. He is:

readLink.label: Read: Impossibility and frustration — s.56 →

options.text: right, because performance has become commercially impossible
options.explanation: Commercial impossibility is precisely the ground the courts refuse. The Act asks whether performance is impossible or unlawful, not whether it is profitable.

options.text: right, because the change was outside his control and could not have been foreseen
options.explanation: Lack of foresight and lack of control are not enough; the event must make performance impossible or unlawful.

options.text: right, and the buyer's remedy is limited to restitution under s.65
options.explanation: s.65 operates only once the contract has actually become void. It has not.

options.text: wrong — a rise in cost makes performance onerous, not impossible, and the contract stands
options.explanation: Correct. He must perform or pay damages under s.73; only impossibility or supervening illegality discharges under s.56.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.44 · Release of one joint promisor
questions.stem: Priya, Qasim and Rehana jointly owe Sameer ₹6,00,000. Sameer executes a written release in favour of Priya alone, and then sues Qasim by himself. The maximum amount Sameer can recover from Qasim is:

readLink.label: Read: Joint promisors and appropriation of payments →

options.explanation: Correct. s.44 says the release of one joint promisor does not discharge the others, and s.43 lets the promisee compel any one of them to perform the whole promise. Qasim's remedy is contribution, including from Priya, whose release does not free her from that.

options.text: ₹4,00,000, Priya's one-third share falling out of the claim on her release
options.explanation: This treats the release as a partial discharge of the debt. s.44 says expressly that it is not.

options.text: ₹2,00,000, being Qasim's own one-third share
options.explanation: This applies English several liability. In India s.43 makes each joint promisor answerable for the whole to the promisee.

options.text: Nil, the release of one joint promisor discharging all of them
options.explanation: That is the English rule that s.44 was written to displace.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.61 · Appropriation where neither party appropriates
questions.stem: Ganesh owes Harpal three distinct debts: ₹18,000 incurred on 12 January 2025, ₹25,000 incurred on 4 March 2025, and ₹15,000 incurred on 20 June 2025. On 1 August 2025 Ganesh pays ₹30,000 without any intimation, and Harpal makes no appropriation either. The amount still outstanding on the ₹25,000 debt is:

readLink.label: Read: Joint promisors and appropriation of payments →

options.text: ₹12,069, the payment being applied to the three debts proportionately
options.explanation: Proportionate application is the rule only for debts of EQUAL STANDING. These three were incurred on different dates.

options.text: ₹10,000, the payment being applied to the newest debt first
options.explanation: This inverts s.61, which discharges debts in order of time — oldest first.
Correct. Under s.61 the ₹30,000 discharges the ₹18,000 debt of 12 January first, and the remaining ₹12,000 goes against the ₹25,000 debt of 4 March, leaving ₹13,000.

options.text: ₹25,000, the payment being incapable of appropriation once both parties are silent
options.explanation: s.61 exists precisely to appropriate the payment when both are silent; the money does not sit in suspense.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.60 · Creditor's appropriation to a time-barred debt
questions.stem: Ishita owes Jaswant ₹40,000 on a loan that became time-barred in March 2025 and ₹60,000 on a current loan. On 5 May 2026 she pays ₹40,000 without indicating which debt it is for, and Jaswant appropriates it to the time-barred loan. The amount Jaswant can still recover from Ishita by suit is:

readLink.label: Read: Joint promisors and appropriation of payments →

options.text: ₹20,000, because the payment must be applied to the current loan
options.explanation: This denies the creditor the discretion s.60 gives him. Where the debtor is silent, the creditor may apply the payment to any lawful debt actually due, including a time-barred one.
Correct. The ₹40,000 lawfully extinguishes the time-barred debt, which was never recoverable by suit anyway, leaving the whole ₹60,000 current loan outstanding and suable.

options.text: ₹1,00,000, an unappropriated payment being held in suspense and reducing nothing
options.explanation: s.60 requires the payment to be appropriated by the creditor; nothing is held in suspense.

options.text: Nil, the whole balance being barred by limitation
options.explanation: Only the ₹40,000 debt was time-barred. The ₹60,000 loan is current.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.43 · Contribution where a joint promisor defaults
questions.stem: Lokesh, Manoj and Nitin jointly promise to pay Om ₹9,00,000. Om compels Lokesh to pay the whole amount. Nitin is insolvent and can contribute nothing. The amount Lokesh can recover from Manoj is:

readLink.label: Read: Joint promisors and appropriation of payments →

options.text: ₹3,00,000, being Manoj's equal one-third share
options.explanation: This stops halfway. s.43 also requires the remaining solvent promisors to bear the defaulter's share in equal shares.

options.text: ₹9,00,000, Manoj being jointly and severally liable for the whole
options.explanation: Joint and several liability runs towards the PROMISEE. Between co-promisors the rule is equal contribution.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, Manoj having to bear the whole of Nitin's default in addition to his own share
options.explanation: Nitin's ₹3,00,000 default is shared EQUALLY between Lokesh and Manoj, not thrown wholly on Manoj.
Correct. Equal shares are ₹3,00,000 each; Nitin's default of ₹3,00,000 is borne equally by Lokesh and Manoj, so Manoj owes ₹3,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹4,50,000.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · s.39 · Anticipatory breach
questions.stem: On 1 March a seller informs the buyer that he will not deliver on the agreed date of 1 July. The buyer decides to keep the contract alive and wait. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Breach and the measure of damages — ss.39, 73 →

options.text: The buyer loses his right to damages altogether by not rescinding at once
options.explanation: Keeping the contract alive preserves the right to sue on 1 July; it does not extinguish it.

options.text: The buyer may sue immediately, and damages will in any case be measured by the market price on 1 July
options.explanation: If he elects to sue immediately, damages are measured at the date of the breach, not at the date fixed for performance.

options.text: The contract remains alive for the benefit of both parties, so if it is discharged by frustration before 1 July the seller escapes liability, and damages will be measured by the market price on 1 July
options.explanation: Correct. That is the precise risk of electing to wait under s.39, and the reason the election matters.

options.text: The buyer must obtain the court's leave before electing to keep the contract alive
options.explanation: No leave is required; s.39 gives the promisee the election as of right.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · s.73 · Special damages and remoteness
questions.stem: A carrier delays the delivery of a broken mill shaft. The mill owner claims the profits lost while the mill stood idle. He had not told the carrier that the mill could not run without the shaft. The claim will:

readLink.label: Read: Breach and the measure of damages — ss.39, 73 →

options.text: fail, the loss of profits being a special loss recoverable only if the special circumstances had been communicated when the contract was made
options.explanation: Correct. This is the second limb of s.73 and the actual decision in Hadley v Baxendale.

options.text: succeed, because loss of profit always arises naturally in the usual course of things from delayed delivery
options.explanation: A carrier could not naturally suppose that a mill has no spare shaft; that is exactly why the loss is not within the first limb.

options.text: succeed, because s.73 allows compensation for any loss caused by the breach
options.explanation: This ignores the closing sentence of s.73, which excludes remote and indirect loss.

options.text: fail, because damages for loss of profit are never recoverable under the Indian Contract Act
options.explanation: They are recoverable whenever the special circumstances were communicated at the time of contracting.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · s.74 · Compensation where a sum is named
questions.stem: A construction contract names ₹8,00,000 as the sum payable by the contractor on delay. The employer proves an actual loss of ₹11,50,000. The court's award under s.74 will be:

readLink.label: Read: Liquidated damages and penalty — s.74 →

options.text: ₹11,50,000, being the actual loss proved
options.explanation: This ignores the ceiling. s.74 permits reasonable compensation NOT EXCEEDING the amount named.

options.text: ₹19,50,000, being the stipulated sum plus the loss actually suffered
options.explanation: The named sum is not an add-on to damages; it is the outer limit of them.

options.text: ₹3,50,000, being the excess of the proved loss over the stipulated sum
options.explanation: This inverts the section — the excess is exactly the part that cannot be recovered.
Correct. Reasonable compensation is capped at the sum named, so the award is limited to ₹8,00,000.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · s.73 · Exemplary damages
questions.stem: In which of the following will Indian courts award exemplary (vindictive) damages for breach of contract?

readLink.label: Read: Breach and the measure of damages — ss.39, 73 →

options.text: Wherever the breach is deliberate and the defaulting party has profited from it
options.explanation: Deliberateness is not a ground. Indian law compensates for loss; it does not punish for breach.

options.text: Wrongful dishonour of a cheque by a banker where the customer had sufficient funds
options.explanation: Correct. This and breach of a promise to marry are the two recognised exceptions, and here the smaller the cheque the larger the damages, the injury being to credit.

options.text: Wherever the aggrieved party has suffered mental distress of any kind
options.explanation: Damages for distress are awarded only in the narrow class of contracts whose very object was comfort or peace of mind, and they are compensatory, not exemplary.

options.text: Wherever the contract itself provides for exemplary damages
options.explanation: A stipulated sum is governed by s.74 and is cut down to reasonable compensation; it cannot create a punitive award.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · ss.65, 75 · Quantum meruit and rescission
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a claim on quantum meruit is INCORRECT?

readLink.label: Read: Quantum meruit, rescission and other remedies →

options.text: It lies where a contract is discovered to be void or becomes void, under s.65
options.explanation: This is a correct statement of the law, so it is not the answer.

options.text: It lies where one party prevents the other from completing his performance
options.explanation: Correct statement of the law (ss.53 and 67), so it is not the answer.

options.text: It lies for the value of the work actually done, rather than for the contract price or the loss of bargain
options.explanation: Correct statement — that is precisely what 'as much as is earned' means.

options.text: It is available to a party who has himself broken the contract, on the same footing as to the party not in default
options.explanation: Correct choice — this statement is WRONG. The claim ordinarily lies at the instance of the party NOT in default; a defaulter under an indivisible contract badly performed may at most recover the lump sum less a deduction.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U6 · ss.30, 31 · Contingent contract and wager compared
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a contingent contract from a wagering agreement?

readLink.label: Read: Contingent contracts — ss.31 to 36 →

options.text: A contingent contract always relates to a future event, whereas a wager may relate to a past event
options.explanation: Both may relate to a past event whose result the parties do not know; that is not the distinguishing feature.

options.text: In a contingent contract the uncertain event is collateral to a contract in which the parties have a real interest, whereas in a wager the event is the sole determining factor and neither party has any interest beyond the stake
options.explanation: Correct. This is why a fire policy taken by an owner is contingent and a bet on the same fire is a wager.

options.text: A contingent contract requires consideration, whereas a wagering agreement does not
options.explanation: Both involve promises for promises. The defect in a wager is that s.30 declares it void, not that consideration is missing.

options.text: A contingent contract is void unless it is in writing, whereas a wagering agreement is void in all cases
options.explanation: No writing is required for a contingent contract; it is a valid contract subject only to s.36.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U6 · ss.32, 36 · Enforcement of contingent contracts
questions.stem: A contracts to pay B ₹2,00,000 if a specified ship returns to port. The ship sinks at sea. The contract:

readLink.label: Read: Contingent contracts — ss.31 to 36 →

options.text: becomes void, because the contingent event has become impossible
options.explanation: Correct. Under s.32 a contract contingent on an uncertain event happening becomes void when the event becomes impossible.

options.text: must be performed at once, the uncertainty having been resolved
options.explanation: Resolution against the event does not trigger performance; it extinguishes the contract.

options.text: was void ab initio under s.36, because the ship's return was always uncertain
options.explanation: s.36 applies to IMPOSSIBLE events, not merely uncertain ones. The return was uncertain, which is what made it a contingent contract.

options.text: becomes voidable at B's option, with compensation for the loss of his bargain
options.explanation: There is no breach and no defective consent, so nothing is voidable and no compensation lies.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U6 · s.70 · Non-gratuitous act
questions.stem: A tradesman leaves goods at a neighbour's house by mistake. The neighbour, knowing they are not his, uses them as his own. Which is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Quasi-contracts — ss.68 to 72 →

options.text: The neighbour owes nothing, there being no contract between them
options.explanation: s.70 creates an obligation without any contract, precisely to prevent unjust enrichment.

options.text: The neighbour must pay, but only under s.72, the goods having been delivered by mistake
options.explanation: s.72 requires the thing delivered by mistake to be RETURNED. Once the neighbour has consumed the benefit, s.70 governs the claim to compensation.

options.text: The neighbour must compensate the tradesman under s.70, the goods having been delivered lawfully and not gratuitously, and the benefit having been enjoyed
options.explanation: Correct. All three conditions of s.70 — lawful act, no intention to act gratuitously, benefit actually enjoyed — are satisfied.

options.text: The neighbour must pay the price only if he expressly promised to do so after using the goods
options.explanation: No promise is needed. The obligation under s.70 is imposed by law, not agreed.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.4 to 7 · Case: an offer, a counter offer and a revocation by post
questions.case: Anupama, at Jodhpur, posts a letter on 3 August 2026 offering to sell her workshop machinery to Bikram at Guwahati for ₹9,50,000, adding: 'This offer stands until 25 August 2026.' Bikram receives the letter on 7 August. On 10 August Bikram posts a reply: 'I accept, provided you also transfer the spare-parts stock at no extra cost.' Anupama does not reply. On 17 August Bikram posts a second letter: 'Withdraw my earlier condition — I accept your offer as it stands.' That letter reaches Anupama on 21 August. Meanwhile Anupama sold the machinery to Chetna on 15 August, and posted a letter revoking her offer to Bikram on 16 August, which reached Bikram on 20 August. All communications were by ordinary post.

readLink.label: Read: Communication, revocation and lapse — ss.3 to 6 →

questions.stem: The legal effect of Bikram's letter of 10 August is that it is:

options.text: a valid acceptance, the additional request being a mere collateral matter
options.explanation: An acceptance must be absolute and unqualified under s.7(1). A demand for extra goods at no extra cost changes the bargain.

options.text: a counter offer, which puts an end to Anupama's original proposal
options.explanation: Correct. A qualified acceptance is a counter offer, and a counter offer destroys the offer it answers.

options.text: a mere inquiry, which leaves Anupama's offer alive for later acceptance
options.explanation: An inquiry asks whether the offeror would consider a variation. Bikram did not ask — he stipulated, which is a counter offer.

options.text: an acceptance subject to a condition precedent, which Anupama was free to waive
options.explanation: s.7 knows no such category. A condition attached by the acceptor makes the reply a counter offer, not a conditional acceptance the offeror may adopt at leisure.

questions.stem: Did Bikram's letter of 17 August create a contract?

options.text: Yes, on 17 August, when the letter was posted
options.explanation: The postal rule fixes WHEN an acceptance takes effect, but only if there is a live proposal to accept. There was none.

options.text: No — the original proposal had already been destroyed by the counter offer of 10 August, so there was nothing left to accept
options.explanation: Correct. Once destroyed, an offer cannot be revived by the offeree withdrawing his condition; only a fresh offer by Anupama would help.

options.text: Yes, on 21 August, when the letter reached Anupama
options.explanation: This addresses the date and ignores the prior destruction of the offer by the counter offer.

options.text: Yes, because the offer was expressed to stand until 25 August and Bikram accepted within that period
options.explanation: A period fixed for acceptance protects against LAPSE by time; it does not protect an offer already killed by a counter offer.

questions.stem: Suppose instead that Bikram's letter of 10 August had been an unqualified acceptance. Anupama's revocation, posted 16 August and reaching Bikram on 20 August, would then be:

options.text: ineffective, a proposal being revocable only before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the proposer — that is, before the acceptance is posted
options.explanation: Correct. The acceptance was posted on 10 August, so the revocation of 16 August comes far too late.

options.text: effective from 16 August, when Anupama put the revocation in the course of transmission
options.explanation: Despatch completes the communication only as against the SENDER. It binds Bikram only when it reaches him.

options.text: effective from 20 August, when the revocation reached Bikram
options.explanation: The date is right for completion against Bikram, but by then the contract had existed for ten days.

options.text: effective, because Anupama had already sold the machinery to Chetna on 15 August and could no longer perform
options.explanation: Selling to a third party is not a revocation communicated to the offeree; it is a breach waiting to happen.

questions.stem: The statement in Anupama's letter that the offer 'stands until 25 August 2026':

options.text: makes the offer irrevocable until 25 August
options.explanation: An offer left open is not irrevocable unless the promise to keep it open is itself supported by consideration. s.6(1) revocation remains available.

options.text: has no legal effect whatever
options.explanation: It has a clear effect: it fixes the point at which the offer lapses under s.6(2), displacing the 'reasonable time' test.

options.text: fixes the time after which the offer lapses under s.6(2), but does not prevent Anupama from revoking it earlier by notice
options.explanation: Correct. Both propositions are true together, and the combination is what the examiner is testing.

options.text: converts the offer into a standing offer, each acceptance forming a separate contract
options.explanation: A standing offer contemplates repeated orders against it. This offer relates to one identified lot of machinery.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · ss.15 to 19 · Case: three attacks on free consent
questions.case: Dharmesh, aged 71 and recently widowed, is immobile after a stroke and depends entirely on his physiotherapist Esha, who visits daily and manages his household payments. (i) Esha persuades Dharmesh to sell his flat to her for ₹22,00,000 when comparable flats in the building sell for about ₹95,00,000. (ii) Separately, a builder, Farhan, tells Dharmesh that the plumbing of a second flat 'was completely replaced last year'. Farhan knows this is untrue, and Dharmesh buys the flat in reliance on it. (iii) Separately again, Dharmesh's tenant Girish tells him that he will set fire to Dharmesh's shop unless Dharmesh signs a fresh lease at half the market rent. Dharmesh signs.

readLink.label: Read: Coercion and undue influence — ss.15 and 16 →

questions.stem: The sale of the flat to Esha is:

options.text: void ab initio, being an unconscionable bargain
options.explanation: Unconscionability under s.16(3) shifts the burden of proof; it does not make the transaction void.

options.text: valid, since Dharmesh was of sound mind and signed of his own accord
options.explanation: Soundness of mind answers s.12, not s.16. A fully lucid person can still have his will dominated.

options.text: voidable at Dharmesh's option for undue influence, the burden of disproving undue influence lying on Esha
options.explanation: Correct. Esha holds real authority over a man whose capacity is affected by age and bodily distress (s.16(2)(a) and (b)), and the price makes the bargain unconscionable, so s.16(3) shifts the burden.

options.text: voidable for coercion, Esha having exploited Dharmesh's distress
options.explanation: Coercion requires a threat of an act forbidden by penal law or an unlawful detention of property. Neither is present; the pressure came from within the relationship.

questions.stem: Farhan's statement about the plumbing is:

options.text: fraud under s.17(1), making the purchase voidable at Dharmesh's option and entitling him to damages as well
options.explanation: Correct. Farhan suggested as a fact something he did not believe to be true, in order to induce the contract.

options.text: misrepresentation under s.18(1), for which rescission but no damages is available
options.explanation: Misrepresentation requires an honest belief in the truth of the statement. Farhan knew it was false.

options.text: not actionable, because Dharmesh could have discovered the defect with ordinary diligence
options.explanation: The Exception to s.19 rescues a defendant only where consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence; it never rescues active fraud.

options.text: a mere opinion about the condition of the flat, and not a statement of fact
options.explanation: A statement that specified work was carried out in a stated year is a statement of past fact, not an opinion.

questions.stem: The lease signed under Girish's threat is:

options.text: undue influence, Girish being in a position to dominate Dharmesh's will as his tenant
options.explanation: A tenancy creates no presumption of domination, and the pressure applied was an external threat, not relational influence.

options.text: voidable at Dharmesh's option for coercion, and on avoiding it he must restore any benefit received under it
options.explanation: Correct. A threat to commit an act forbidden by the penal law is coercion (s.15); s.19 makes the lease voidable and s.64 requires restoration of benefits.

options.text: not coercion, because the threat was directed at property rather than at any person
options.explanation: s.15's first limb covers threats to commit any act forbidden by the penal law, whatever the target; arson qualifies.

options.text: not coercion, because Girish did not in fact carry out the threat
options.explanation: s.15 covers 'committing, OR THREATENING to commit'. Execution of the threat is not required.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · ss.41, 56, 65 · Case: a shipment, a prohibition and a substitute performer
questions.case: On 10 January 2026 Himalaya Freight Ltd contracts with Kandla Exports Ltd to carry 2,000 tonnes of machinery from Kandla to a named foreign port, shipment on 1 September 2026, freight ₹40,00,000 of which ₹10,00,000 is paid in advance. Consider four separate and independent developments occurring in June 2026: (i) the Government of India prohibits the export of that class of machinery to that country; (ii) marine fuel prices rise by 70%, so that the voyage will now be loss-making for Himalaya; (iii) the particular vessel Himalaya had earmarked for the voyage sinks, though equivalent tonnage is freely available on charter; and (iv) Himalaya's sister company performs the carriage instead, and Kandla Exports accepts that performance without objection.

readLink.label: Read: Impossibility and frustration — s.56 →

questions.stem: The effect of the export prohibition in (i) is that:

options.text: the contract becomes voidable at Himalaya's option
options.explanation: Supervening illegality gives nobody an option; it terminates the contract by operation of s.56.

options.text: the contract continues, and Himalaya must find some lawful means of performing it
options.explanation: There is no lawful means left. The very act promised has been prohibited.

options.text: the contract is void ab initio under the first paragraph of s.56
options.explanation: The first paragraph deals with an act impossible IN ITSELF when the agreement is made. This act was perfectly possible in January.

options.text: the contract becomes void under the second paragraph of s.56, and the ₹10,00,000 advance is restorable under s.65
options.explanation: Correct. The act became unlawful by an event Himalaya could not prevent, and s.65 requires the advantage received to be restored.

questions.stem: The rise in fuel prices in (ii):

options.text: frustrates the contract, performance having become commercially impossible
options.explanation: Commercial impossibility is the classic non-ground. The Act asks about impossibility, not profitability.

options.text: does not frustrate the contract; Himalaya must perform or pay damages under s.73
options.explanation: Correct. Increased cost makes performance onerous, not impossible.

options.text: entitles Himalaya to a proportionate increase in freight under s.62
options.explanation: s.62 permits alteration only by AGREEMENT of the parties; it confers no unilateral right to revise the price.

options.text: makes the contract voidable at Himalaya's option under s.55
options.explanation: s.55 concerns failure to perform within a stipulated time, and gives the option to the PROMISEE, not to the defaulting promisor.

questions.stem: The sinking of the earmarked vessel in (iii):

options.text: frustrates the contract, the subject matter having been destroyed
options.explanation: The subject matter of the contract is the carriage of the cargo, not the particular ship, which was merely the means Himalaya had chosen.

options.text: frustrates the contract only because a ship is a thing of a special character
options.explanation: Nothing in s.56 turns on the character of the means of performance; the question is whether performance itself is now impossible.

options.text: does not frustrate the contract, because the promise was to carry the cargo and substitute tonnage is freely available, so performance remains possible
options.explanation: Correct. Destruction of the chosen means is not destruction of the subject matter where an alternative means exists.

options.text: discharges Himalaya under s.40, performance having become personal to the vessel
options.explanation: s.40 protects contracts requiring the PROMISOR's personal skill, taste or credit. A freight contract is not one of them.

questions.stem: After the events in (iv), can Kandla Exports afterwards enforce the carriage obligation against Himalaya?

options.text: No — s.41 provides that a promisee who accepts performance from a third person cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor
options.explanation: Correct. Acceptance of the third party's performance is final, and it discharges the promisor even though he never consented to the substitution.

options.text: Yes, because Himalaya never agreed to the substitution of its sister company
options.explanation: The promisor's consent is irrelevant under s.41; what matters is the promisee's acceptance.

options.text: Yes, unless the parties had novated the contract under s.62
options.explanation: Novation is a different route to discharge and requires everyone's agreement. s.41 discharges the promisor without any novation.

options.text: No, but only if Himalaya had authorised the sister company in writing
options.explanation: s.41 requires no authority and no writing. The promisee's acceptance is the whole of the operative fact.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · ss.73, 74 · Case: measuring damages for non-delivery
questions.case: On 5 May 2026 Tanvi Textiles agrees to supply 800 metres of a specified fabric to Ujjwal Garments at ₹450 per metre, delivery on 5 July 2026. The contract names ₹2,00,000 as the sum payable by the seller on failure to deliver. Tanvi fails to deliver on 5 July, when the market rate for the fabric is ₹520 per metre. Ujjwal does nothing for six weeks and finally buys a substitute on 20 August at ₹575 per metre. Ujjwal had an export order for the finished garments which would have yielded a margin equivalent to ₹800 per metre of fabric; that order was never disclosed to Tanvi.

readLink.label: Read: Breach and the measure of damages — ss.39, 73 →

questions.stem: The ordinary (general) damages recoverable by Ujjwal under the first limb of s.73 are:

options.explanation: Correct. 800 metres × (₹520 market rate on the date of breach − ₹450 contract rate) = ₹56,000, which is the loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things.
This uses the 20 August substitute rate of ₹575 and so charges Tanvi with the consequences of Ujjwal's own delay.
This is the export margin of ₹350 per metre, which is a special loss and not ordinary damages at all.
This is the extra cost caused by the delay in buying a substitute — the very part of the loss that Ujjwal cannot recover.

questions.stem: The amount of the substitute-purchase cost that Ujjwal CANNOT recover, because of the duty to mitigate, is:

options.text: Nil — the whole cost of the substitute purchase is recoverable once a breach is proved
options.explanation: The Explanation to s.73 requires the means of remedying the inconvenience to be taken into account; a loss the claimant could reasonably have avoided is not recoverable.
That is the whole differential measured from the contract price to the 20 August rate, not the avoidable part of it.
Correct. 800 metres × (₹575 on 20 August − ₹520 on the date of breach) = ₹44,000, which Ujjwal could have avoided by buying a substitute within a reasonable time.
That is the recoverable ordinary damages, not the irrecoverable avoidable loss.

questions.stem: Ujjwal's claim for the lost export margin will:

options.text: succeed, because loss of profit on resale always arises naturally from a failure to deliver
options.explanation: A seller cannot be assumed to know of a particular export order; that is why the second limb requires communication.

options.text: succeed, because Tanvi could have foreseen that garment fabric would be resold at a profit
options.explanation: General foreseeability of some resale is not enough; the SPECIAL circumstances must have been made known when the contract was made.

options.text: succeed to the extent of a reasonable ordinary profit, though not the full export margin
options.explanation: s.73 does not offer a halfway house of this kind. The loss is either within a limb of the section or it is not recoverable.

options.text: fail, the export order being a special circumstance which was never communicated to Tanvi when the contract was made
options.explanation: Correct. This is the second limb of s.73 and the rule in Hadley v Baxendale.

questions.stem: The effect of the ₹2,00,000 named in the contract is that:

options.text: Ujjwal is entitled to ₹2,00,000 automatically, actual loss being irrelevant
options.explanation: The words 'whether or not actual damage or loss is proved' relieve the claimant of a technical failure of proof; they do not turn the named sum into an entitlement.

options.text: Ujjwal is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding ₹2,00,000, so on these facts he recovers ₹56,000
options.explanation: Correct. Under s.74 the named sum operates only as a ceiling, and India draws no distinction between liquidated damages and a penalty.

options.text: the clause is void as a penalty, and Ujjwal must prove his loss under s.73 alone
options.explanation: s.74 does not strike such clauses down; it cuts them down to reasonable compensation.

options.text: Ujjwal may claim ₹2,00,000 in addition to the damages computed under s.73
options.explanation: The named sum replaces, and caps, the damages; it is never added to them.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.2(a), 6, 7 · Offer and invitation to offer
questions.stem: Define a 'proposal' under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the legal rules relating to a valid offer, and distinguish an offer from an invitation to offer with suitable examples. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Definition: signifying to another one's willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence

Rules for a valid offer: must intend to create legal relations; terms must be certain; must be communicated to the offeree; conditions must be brought to the offeree's notice; must not stipulate that silence shall amount to acceptance

Kinds of offer: express and implied; specific (Boulton v Jones) and general (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co); cross offers, which form no contract; counter offer, which destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench); standing or continuing offer

Invitation to offer: it invites the other party to make the offer, the person issuing it retaining the power to accept or refuse — shop-window display, self-service shelves, auction announcements, tender notices, prospectus, catalogue and price list

Practical consequence, with an example: the customer at the counter and the bidder at an auction are the offerors, so a bid may be withdrawn before the fall of the hammer and a shopkeeper may refuse to sell a displayed article at the marked price

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U1 · ss.3 to 6 · Communication and revocation
questions.stem: State the rules relating to the communication and revocation of a proposal and of an acceptance under sections 3 to 6, explaining when each communication is complete and the time within which a revocation must be made. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: s.3 — communication is made by any act or omission of the party by which he intends to communicate, or which has the effect of communicating it
s.4 — communication of a PROPOSAL is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made

s.4 — communication of an ACCEPTANCE is complete as against the proposer when it is put in a course of transmission to him so as to be out of the acceptor's power, and as against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer

s.4 — communication of a REVOCATION is complete as against the person making it when it is put into a course of transmission, and as against the person to whom it is made when it comes to his knowledge
