s.5 — a proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer (that is, before the acceptance is posted); an acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor (that is, before it reaches the proposer)

s.6 — a proposal is revoked by notice of revocation; by lapse of the time prescribed or of a reasonable time; by failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent; and by the death or insanity of the proposer if that fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance. Add: telephone and other instantaneous communication carry no transmission gap, so the contract is complete only when the acceptance is heard

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U2 · s.25 · No consideration, no contract
questions.stem: 'An agreement made without consideration is void.' State the rule and explain the exceptions to it under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: The rule and the definition: consideration means an act, abstinence or promise, at the desire of the promisor, by the promisee or any other person; an agreement without consideration is void

Exception 1 — natural love and affection: the agreement must be in writing, registered, made between parties standing in a near relation to each other, and made on account of natural love and affection; all four elements are cumulative
Exception 2 — past voluntary service: a promise to compensate a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something the promisor was legally compellable to do

Exception 3 — time-barred debt: a promise in writing, signed by the person to be charged or his authorised agent, to pay wholly or in part a debt the creditor might have enforced but for the law of limitation
Explanations: a completed gift between donor and donee is unaffected; and inadequacy of consideration does not make an agreement void, though it is evidence on the question of free consent

Other situations where consideration is not required: creation of an agency; remission or extension of time by a promisee; gratuitous bailment; and a charitable subscription on the faith of which the promisee has incurred a liability (Kedar Nath Bhattacharji v Gorie Mahomed)

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · ss.11, 12, 68 · Capacity to contract
questions.stem: Explain the legal position of an agreement entered into by a minor under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and state briefly who else is incompetent to contract. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: s.11 — three tests of competence: age of majority (18 years under the Indian Majority Act 1875), soundness of mind, and not being disqualified by any law

An agreement with a minor is void ab initio, so neither the money advanced nor the security can be recovered (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose); and it cannot be ratified on attaining majority — a fresh contract with fresh consideration is required
skeleton.citation: s. 11; Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose

skeleton.point: A minor may be a promisee or beneficiary and may enforce a contract for his benefit; he may act as an agent without personal liability; he may be admitted to the benefits of a partnership with the consent of all the partners; he cannot be adjudicated insolvent; and there is no estoppel against him where he has misrepresented his age, though a court may on equitable principles order restoration of what is still traceable in his hands

Necessaries: where a person incapable of contracting, or anyone he is legally bound to support, is supplied with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the supplier is reimbursed from the property of that incapable person — a quasi-contractual claim against the estate, never a personal decree

Persons of unsound mind: soundness is tested at the time the contract is made — a person usually of unsound mind may contract during a lucid interval, and a person usually of sound mind may not contract while temporarily insane; idiocy, lunacy, delirium, drunkenness and hypnotism are covered

Disqualified persons: alien enemies during a war; foreign sovereigns and diplomats, who cannot be sued without the Central Government's sanction; convicts undergoing sentence; adjudicated insolvents; and corporations acting beyond their memorandum or governing statute

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U3 · ss.15, 16 · Coercion and undue influence distinguished
questions.stem: Distinguish between coercion and undue influence under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Coercion defined: committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the penal law, or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement

Undue influence defined: where the relations between the parties are such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage; domination is deemed where there is real or apparent authority or a fiduciary relation, or where the other's mental capacity is affected by age, illness, or mental or bodily distress

Nature and source of the pressure: coercion is physical or penal and may be applied by any person against any person, including a stranger to the contract; undue influence is moral or mental and arises from a relationship between the contracting parties themselves

Burden of proof: in coercion the party alleging it must prove it; in undue influence, once domination is shown and the transaction appears unconscionable, the burden of proving the absence of undue influence shifts to the dominant party

Effect and relief: both make the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party; on rescission for coercion the benefit received must be restored and money paid is recoverable, whereas for undue influence the court may set the contract aside absolutely or upon such terms as it thinks just

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U4 · s.56 · Supervening impossibility
questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of supervening impossibility under section 56, stating the events which do and do not discharge a contract, and the consequence of the contract becoming void. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: The three limbs of s.56: an agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void; a contract to do an act which afterwards becomes impossible, or by reason of some event the promisor could not prevent becomes unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful; and a promisor who knew or with reasonable diligence might have known of the impossibility, where the promisee did not, must compensate the promisee

Events that DO discharge: destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell); death or incapacity where personal performance is required; change of law or supervening illegality; non-occurrence of the state of things forming the foundation of the contract (Krell v Henry); and outbreak of war

Events that do NOT discharge: mere difficulty of performance; commercial impossibility such as a steep rise in cost or the contract becoming unprofitable; default of a third party; strikes, lock-outs and civil disturbance unless expressly provided for; self-induced impossibility; and failure of one of several objects

Consequence: when a contract becomes void, any person who has received an advantage under it must restore it or make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it — so advances come back and there is no claim for the lost bargain

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U5 · ss.73, 74 · Damages for breach
questions.stem: State the rules relating to the measure of damages for breach of contract under section 73, and explain the Indian position on a sum named in the contract as payable on breach under section 74. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: s.73 — the aggrieved party is entitled to compensation for loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach (ordinary or general damages), or which the parties knew when they made the contract to be likely to result from the breach (special damages); this is the rule in Hadley v Baxendale in statutory form
Remoteness: no compensation is given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach

Duty to mitigate: the Explanation requires the means that existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by non-performance to be taken into account, so a loss the aggrieved party could reasonably have avoided is not recoverable, though the reasonable cost of mitigating is

Kinds of damages: ordinary damages, measured in a sale by the difference between the contract price and the market price on the date of breach; special damages on prior communication of the special circumstances; nominal damages where a right is infringed without loss; and exemplary damages only for breach of a promise to marry and for wrongful dishonour of a cheque by a banker

s.74 — where a sum is named in the contract, or a stipulation by way of penalty is contained in it, the aggrieved party is entitled, whether or not actual damage is proved, to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named; India draws no distinction between liquidated damages and a penalty, and the named sum operates only as a ceiling

s.74 Explanation and Exception: a stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a penalty; and a person who gives a bail bond, recognizance or other bond under the law, or a bond under a direction of the Government for the performance of a public duty, is liable on breach to pay the whole sum named

questions.topic: Ch 2 · U6 · ss.30 to 36 · Contingent contracts
questions.stem: Define a contingent contract, state the rules governing its enforcement under sections 32 to 36, and distinguish it from a wagering agreement. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Definition and essentials: a contract to do or not to do something if some event, collateral to the contract, does or does not happen; the event must be a future uncertain event, collateral to the contract, and not the mere will of the promisor. Contracts of insurance, indemnity and guarantee are contingent contracts

ss.32 and 33: a contract contingent on an uncertain future event HAPPENING cannot be enforced unless and until the event has happened, and becomes void if the event becomes impossible; a contract contingent on an event NOT happening can be enforced when the happening of the event becomes impossible, and not before

ss.34 and 35: where the event is the future conduct of a living person, it is deemed impossible when that person does anything which renders it impossible that he should so act within any definite time or otherwise than under further contingencies; where a time is fixed, the contract becomes void if the time expires without the event or the event becomes impossible earlier, and a contract contingent on the event NOT happening within the fixed time may be enforced when the time expires without it, or earlier if it becomes certain that the event will not happen
s.36: contingent agreements to do or not to do anything if an impossible event happens are void, whether or not the impossibility of the event was known to the parties when the agreement was made

Distinction from a wager: a contingent contract is valid whereas a wagering agreement is void; in a contingent contract the event is collateral to a transaction in which the parties have a real interest, whereas in a wager the event is the sole determining factor and neither party has any interest beyond the stake; a wager requires mutual chances of gain and loss, which a contingent contract does not; and the parties to a wager have no control over the event
